system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-01-10 18:24:00 to 2184-01-21 20:14:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with fever and hypotension during dialysis, found to have MSSA bacteremia likely from his right femoral dialysis catheter. He was treated with vancomycin initially, then transitioned to cefazolin after sensitivities confirmed susceptibility. The infected catheter was removed, and after a 5-day line holiday, a new tunneled left femoral dialysis catheter was placed. Blood cultures cleared, and he completed dialysis without complications. His heart function remained stable, and no endocarditis was detected. New medications were started, including lisinopril for heart failure, atorvastatin, and adjusted phosphate binders. He was discharged to an extended care facility on outpatient antibiotics with plans for ongoing dialysis and follow-up.
problems: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to other vascular device, implant, and graft
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy

INDICATION:  ___ male with end-stage renal disease and tunneled left
femoral dialysis line presenting with Staph bacteremia.  Request for catheter
removal with culture of the line tip.

OPERATORS:  The procedure was performed by Dr. ___ (fellow).  Dr.
___ attending radiologist, reviewed the study.  

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  A timeout was performed with two patient identifiers.
The patient's indwelling dialysis catheter and left groin were prepped and
draped in usual sterile fashion.  Approximately 10 cc of lidocaine was
administered to the tunneled site.  Blunt dissection was performed around the
catheter cuff.  Gentle pressure was used to remove the catheter and pressure
was placed at the left common femoral venous entry site for approximately ten
minutes.  A sterile dressing was applied over the puncture site.  The tip of
the catheter was sent for culture.  There were no post-procedural
complications.

IMPRESSION:  Successful removal of a tunneled left common femoral hemodialysis
catheter.  The tip was sent for culture.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ male with end-stage renal disease on
hemodialysis, presenting with sepsis.  Request for placement of a temporary
femoral HD line with VIP port.

OPERATORS:  The procedure was performed by Dr. ___ (fellow).  Dr.
___, the attending radiologist, supervised and reviewed the
study.

ANESTHESIA:  1% local lidocaine.  The patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored throughout the course of the procedure.

PROCEDURE:  After the risks, benefits and alternatives of the procedure were
explained to the patient, informed consent was obtained.  The patient was
brought to the angiographic suite and his right groin was prepped and draped
in the usual sterile fashion.  A preprocedure timeout and huddle were
performed as per ___ protocol.

Under ultrasound guidance with hard copy images on file, the right common
femoral vein was accessed with a 19-gauge needle over the femoral head.  A
___ wire was advanced into the IVC and serial dilatations were performed
over the wire.  A 12 ___ peel-away sheath was then placed over the wire and
the guidewire and inner dilator were removed.  A new 12 ___ dual-lumen
hemodialysis catheter with VIP port measuring 20 cm in length was advanced
over the wire and the wire was removed.  All three ports were aspirated and
flushed easily.  The catheter was secured to the skin with 0 silk suture and a
sterile dressing was applied.  A final fluoroscopic image was saved digitally
and confirmed satisfactory position of the catheter with the tip terminating
in the proximal right common iliac vein.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

IMPRESSION:  Successful placement of a 12 ___ dual-lumen temporary dialysis
catheter with VIP port measuring 20 cm in length via right common femoral
venous access. The line is ready for use.

MEDICAL HISTORY:  ___ man with end-stage renal disease and MRSA
bacteremia.  A left tunneled femoral dialysis catheter was removed about a
week ago and a temporary right femoral HD catheter was removed two days ago. 
Patient has a history of central occlusion of the veins in the neck and upper
chest.  A femoral tunneled hemodialysis catheter placement was requested.

COMPARISON:  Multiple similar procedures in the past.

CLINICIANS:  Dr. ___, Dr. ___, and Dr. ___.  Dr.
___ is the attending radiologist who was present and supervising
throughout.

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
200 mcg of fentanyl and 2.5 mg of Versed throughout the total intra-service
time of 1 hour 30 minutes, during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters
were continuously monitored.  Local anesthesia with 1% lidocaine and lidocaine
with epinephrine.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  An informed written consent was obtained after
explaining the procedure, benefits, alternatives and risks involved.  Patient
was brought to angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  The
left groin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  A
preprocedure huddle and timeout were performed as per ___ protocol.

Under ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance with hard copy images of ultrasound
on file, the left common femoral vein was accessed with a micropuncture set. 
Through the micropuncture sheath, a 0.035 ___ wire was placed and advanced
into right atrium.  Appropriate measurements were then obtained for the
catheter length.  Then after instilling 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, a small
incision was made over the anterolateral upper thigh.  From this incision, a
50-cm tip-to-cuff tunneled hemodialysis catheter was placed and brought out at
the venotomy site using the tunneling device.  Then after removing the
micropuncture sheath, the soft tissue tract was dilated with serial dilators
over the guidewire.  A peel-away sheath was placed over the guidewire.  The
inner dilator and guidewire were removed and the catheter was placed through
the peel-away sheath and advanced into right atrium.  The peel-away sheath was
then removed.  Catheter secured to skin with 0 silk sutures and venotomy site
closed with ___ Vicryl suture.  Both ports of the catheter were easily
aspirated and flushed.  A fluoroscopic spot chest film was obtained
demonstrating satisfactory position and placement of the catheter with the tip
terminating in the right atrium.  Sterile dressings were applied.  Patient
tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:  Successful placement of a tunneled hemodialysis catheter
measuring 50 cm tip-to-cuff via left common femoral venous access with the tip
of the catheter terminating in the right atrium.  The line is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with fevers and shaking during dialysis today. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still tired… I had chills bad during dialysis. Felt like I was freezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your temperature was 103.5 when you arrived. We’ve started antibiotics—vancomycin and gentamicin—for a possible infection from your dialysis line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I had that last fall…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your history. We’re concerned it might be happening again. Your blood cultures are growing something, and we’ll know more soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My dad just passed… I didn’t even go to the funeral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m very sorry to hear that. We’ve let social work know, and they’ll check in with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show elevated white blood cells and your potassium is a bit high, but your heart and lungs look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it the same bug as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s Staph aureus again, but this time it’s MRSA—methicillin-resistant. That means we need to stick with vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So same antibiotic as last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we can’t switch to cefazolin like last time because this strain is resistant. Vancomycin will stay for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my line? Do they have to take it out again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discussing that. There was pus at the site, so it’s likely the source. Infectious disease recommends removing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We removed your femoral dialysis line this morning. The tip will be cultured to confirm the infection source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So how will I get dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a temporary line soon. You’ll have a short break—called a line holiday—before the new one goes in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least 24 hours. We want to make sure no bacteria spread during placement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood pressure stabilized after we held your lisinopril. You were a bit shaky yesterday, so we moved you to the ICU for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember that…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were very sleepy. We gave fluids and your vitals improved. Your temporary dialysis line was placed yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can dialyze now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a session yesterday. We’re watching your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest blood culture still showed MRSA. We’re keeping the temporary line out for a few more days to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I thought removing the line would help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, but sometimes bacteria linger. We’re doing another 72-hour break to let your blood clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram yesterday. No sign of infection on your heart valves—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it have spread there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were worried about endocarditis, but the echo was clean. Your ejection fraction is about 30%, which is low but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no worsening. We’ll keep you on digoxin and aspirin. Lisinopril will restart when you’re fully stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures today are negative. That’s a great sign—the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m clear?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep checking, but this is very encouraging. We’re planning to place your new permanent line soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling your new tunneled femoral catheter for tomorrow. It’ll go in the left side this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same spot as last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re using ultrasound and fluoroscopy to guide it. The team reviewed your history of clots and narrowed veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your new dialysis line was placed yesterday. It’s working well, and you’ve had one session already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more temporary lines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is your new permanent one. We’ll keep vancomycin for four weeks total to make sure the infection is fully treated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll take it at dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’ll be given during each session. You’ll need weekly blood tests—CBC and vancomycin levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest culture is still negative. We’re on track for discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To an extended care facility. They’ll help with your recovery and coordinate your dialysis and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I see my regular doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll follow up with nephrology and infectious disease. We’ll send all your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge meds. Lisinopril is back on your list, and we’ve adjusted your phosphate binders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My seizure meds are the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oxcarbazepine and levetiracetam continue. We lowered the oxcarbazepine dose slightly due to interactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your temperature and the dialysis site daily. Call if you see redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds in a day, let your team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue vancomycin with dialysis for four weeks total. The facility will handle the infusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, weekly CBC and vancomycin troughs. The results go to the infectious disease clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’ve got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The social worker will go over everything again before you leave. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my stomach’s been off. Is that the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be. We’ve added senna and bisacodyl for constipation, which is common with pain patches and some antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If diarrhea continues, let the facility know. We don’t want you getting dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking the omeprazole. It helps protect your stomach, especially with all these meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. It’s important, especially with your history of GI bleeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—my heart. Is it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart function is stable. EF is 30%, which is low, but no signs of worsening. Keep taking your meds and stay on dialysis schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep following the plan, and we’ll get you through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will be in shortly with your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with fevers and hypotension during dialysis, found to have MRSA bacteremia likely originating from his right femoral dialysis catheter. He was treated with vancomycin and initially retained the line despite purulence, but developed hypotension requiring MICU care. The infected catheter was removed, followed by a temporary line and two line holidays due to persistent positive cultures. Surveillance cultures eventually cleared, and a new tunneled left femoral dialysis catheter was placed. Echocardiograms showed no evidence of endocarditis, and heart function remained stable. The patient completed antibiotic therapy with vancomycin dosed through dialysis, and was discharged to an extended care facility on a four-week course with weekly monitoring of CBC and vancomycin levels. He restarted lisinopril and continued management of comorbidities including ESRD, systolic heart failure, and seizure disorder.
